meta.title: The overnight queue backlog and the restart that made it worse
meta.subtitle: A site reliability engineer and the platform engineer who shipped the config change walk through how a four-connection typo turned into a duplicate-email incident.

abstract: Nadia Brandt and Colm Ferreira reconstruct an overnight outage. A connection-pool change Colm meant to scope to one queue lands on the ingest fleet's shared default, and when nightly batch volume rises the workers cannot keep pace; backlog climbs for half an hour before an alert pages Nadia. Seeing healthy workers, she restarts the fleet, which triggers a reconnect storm and redelivers unacknowledged messages, so customers receive duplicate confirmation emails. Colm eventually traces the outage to his own change, and after coordinating a safe revert the backlog drains. The pair leave with next steps on message deduplication, a config guardrail, a reconnect limit, and confirming what customers were told.

acts.title: The change and the silent climb
acts.summary: A connection-pool change meant for a different queue lands on the shared ingest default; when nightly batch volume rises the workers cannot keep pace, and the queue depth climbs for nearly half an hour before the alert pages Nadia.

turning_point.text: backlog is flat, flat, flat, and then it just starts climbing at 0214 UTC.

acts.title: The restart makes it worse
acts.summary: Seeing healthy-looking workers, Nadia restarts the ingest fleet; the simultaneous reconnect spikes the config service and redelivers unacknowledged messages, which the notification service resends as duplicate confirmation emails to customers.

turning_point.text: Killing the process before the ack means the queue thinks that message was never delivered, so it redelivers it once a worker comes back.

acts.title: Root cause, revert, and the next steps
acts.summary: Colm traces the outage to his own misapplied config change, and after confirming it is safe to revert, the two coordinate a fix; the backlog drains and the pair sets next steps on dedupe, guardrails and comms.

turning_point.text: 0338 UTC. I'm confident on that one, I've got the terminal history and the diff right in front of me, timestamped.

threads.name: The scoped config change that wasn't scoped
threads.what: Colm's connection-pool change was meant for one queue's config key but landed on the shared default the ingest fleet also reads.
threads.why_it_matters: That mistake is the root cause of the entire night, from the backlog to the duplicate emails.

threads.name: Restart without idempotent redelivery
threads.what: Nadia restarted the ingest fleet while workers held unacknowledged messages, and the notification service resent confirmations on redelivery.
threads.why_it_matters: The restart, not the original backlog, is what made the incident customer-visible.

threads.name: Who told the customers
threads.what: Neither Nadia nor Colm can confirm what, if anything, customers who received duplicate emails were told.
threads.why_it_matters: It is an open item that could leave customer-facing teams caught out if a customer asks.

evidence.claim: The connection-pool change that ultimately caused the backlog shipped at 0148 UTC.
evidence.evidence: Colm reads the exact time directly off the deploy log while on the call.

evidence.claim: Colm identified his own config change as the root cause at 0338 UTC.
evidence.evidence: He has the terminal history and the diff open in front of him, timestamped, while speaking.

evidence.claim: The queue backlog reached zero at 0455 UTC.
evidence.evidence: Nadia posted that exact timestamp to the incident channel the moment the alert cleared, and reads it back from that log.

evidence.claim: The queue depth chart shows backlog starting to climb right at 0214 UTC.
evidence.evidence: Nadia read this off the queue depth chart before the call, a real dashboard, but is presenting her own reading of the graph rather than a saved snapshot.

evidence.claim: Restarting the fleet caused a connection storm against the config service.
evidence.evidence: Nadia watched the connection count spike live while it happened, but has no saved graph of it in front of her now.

evidence.claim: The queue depth number Nadia saw when first paged was far above anything she'd consider normal.
evidence.evidence: She is recalling the figure from memory at three in the morning and admits she never wrote it down.

evidence.claim: Customers began receiving duplicate confirmation emails around 0311 UTC.
evidence.evidence: Nadia heard this secondhand from someone on the support team and was not watching the clock when it happened.

evidence.claim: A note was sent to customers explaining the duplicate confirmation emails.
evidence.evidence: Colm says he believes someone in comms sent something but has not seen it and was not involved.

signals.signal: Colm apologizes for not adding a rate-based alert after a past incident; Nadia waves it off and redirects to the timeline.
Nadia corrects her own memory of the restart time from roughly three o'clock down to 0258 UTC after checking the runbook log.

numbers.means: Max connections per worker, before and after Colm's config change.
Connections each worker resumes using within a minute or two of the revert, per Colm.

quotes.speaker: N
quotes.text: let's just walk through the whole night in order, start to finish

quotes.speaker: C
quotes.text: the reasoning was, we'd been leaning on a different queue's database pretty hard during a migration earlier in the week

quotes.speaker: N
quotes.text: Killing the process before the ack means the queue thinks that message was never delivered, so it redelivers it once a worker comes back.

quotes.speaker: C
quotes.text: you can't restart a fleet that has unacknowledged in-flight work without expecting redelivery

quotes.speaker: N
quotes.text: a restart can happen for a dozen legitimate reasons that have nothing to do with your config change

tensions.note: Nadia and Colm disagree about which fix matters more, notification-service idempotency versus restart-time guardrails, and timebox rather than resolve it.

diarization.why: Colm's two-word reaction lands right at Nadia's pause; diarization places it as a separate turn but it could be a brief overlap.

next_steps.commitment: Colm to add a dedupe key to the notification service so redelivery is a no-op instead of a second email.
Colm to put a floor under the connection-pool default so it cannot be set below a safe minimum.
Colm to add a reconnect rate limit so a full fleet restart staggers instead of reconnecting all at once.
Someone to confirm with the comms owner exactly what customers who received duplicate emails were told.

aligned_on: The restart, not the original backlog, is what made the incident customer-visible.
The connection-pool change landing on the shared default is the root cause.
unresolved: Whether notification-service idempotency or restart-time guardrails matters more as the primary fix.
What, if anything, customers were told about the duplicate emails.

risks.note: She is relying on memory for the exact queue depth figure and the time she first heard about the duplicate emails, both from a three a.m. shift.
He has not confirmed the customer communication and is passing along something he only heard about in passing.
